per_pair.why: B's forest clearing has organic grass edges, layered pines, flowers, mushrooms, a lily-padded pond and a cosmic backdrop that make it feel placed by hand, while A is a symmetric dark-stone rectangle whose two warm lamp pools are the only points of interest.

B mixes irregular water cutouts, a dirt patch, a hand-painted sign and lush foliage into a varied, readable space, whereas A's checker-tile floor with a red carpet is busy, low in contrast and again built from the same mirrored pillar-and-lamp layout.

B's stone room has distinct cobbled wall courses, flickering wall torches, fallen pillars and a mixed-material floor with clear depth, while A's stone room is a flat, near-monochrome purple slab where the floor, walls and props blur together.

A gives a readable completion beat (an ARENA CLEARED banner, the top gate glowing and lifting, sparks, and lit markers by the bottom gate), while B's strip is a plain checkerboard void with a typewriter text box and no visible way onward opening.

loser_biggest_gap: Break A's rooms out of the single symmetric dark-stone template: give each arena its own layout silhouette (non-rectangular edges, pits or water cutouts, raised ledges) and a distinct material and color palette, so rooms read as individually designed places and not recolored copies of one box.
loser_other_gaps: Increase value contrast between floor, walls and props: right now the floor tiles, wall blocks and furniture all sit in the same dark purple-grey band, so the space reads as mush at a glance.
Add hand-placed set dressing with storytelling (rubble, broken pillars, banners with variation, plants growing through cracks, signs) instead of evenly scattered small clutter at the wall edges.
Vary lighting beyond two identical warm lamp pools per room: add colored or flickering light sources, rim light on walls, and darker corners to create depth and focal points.
Give walls real height and depth (top caps, cast shadows onto the floor, a front-wall occlusion layer) so rooms stop looking like a flat top-down floor plan.
reasoning: Across the three combat stills, B's environments look far more deliberately composed: organic boundaries, layered foliage, readable floor materials, characterful props and lighting that guides the eye, all with strong value separation. A is cohesive and tidy, but every room reuses the same symmetric dark-stone box with two lamp pools and a gate, and its low-contrast palette makes the spaces feel flat and samey. A's door-slam strip is a better completion moment, with a clear banner and a visible gate opening, while B's strip shows a bland checkerboard void. That one strong beat does not outweigh B's consistently more handcrafted and inviting levels.
